sentences.text: Sinornis was described in 1992 as a skeleton roughly the size of a modern sparrow that combined ancient traits with those of modern birds.
Its skeleton shares remarkable basal features with Archaeopteryx, an early transitional bird.
The animal possessed moderately recurved manual claws, which were less curved than the high-recurved claws found in Archaeopteryx.
Like Archaeopteryx, the pubis of Sinornis was directed ventrally and ended in a hook-shaped structure resembling a boot.
The forelimb featured a separate carpus and manus, unlike the fused bones found in modern birds.
The pelvis included a footed pubis bone.
Evidence suggests the creature was capable of both perching and climbing.
It had separate finger bones adapted for flight and a reduced tail that shifted the center of gravity forward.
Based on its skeleton, Sinornis shared flight and perching capabilities similar to modern sparrow-sized birds living in arboreal habitats.
Sinornis is classified under the class Reptilia.
In 2001, Paul Sereno and colleagues considered the species Cathayornis to be a junior synonym of Sinornis due to their similar anatomy.
In 2001, Zhou and Hou argued that Cathayornis and Sinornis are distinct genera, citing differences in size, finger structure, and claw length.
Sinornis lived during the Lower Cretaceous period in the Jiufotang Formation of China.
Sinornis lived during the Aptian stage, between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
Later research revised the age of the Sinornis fossil layers to 120 to 110 million years old, which reduced its perceived importance in the timeline of avian evolution.
